```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7, fig.height = 3.2)
```

```{r setup}
library(cortisol.nmea)
```

The workflow removes a sample when its absolute residual from the initial fit is
larger than a cutoff. A low cutoff removes more contamination but also more good
samples; with only four or five samples per person, each wrongly removed sample
costs a lot, and a person left with fewer than three is excluded altogether.

## The rule

The cutoff is $k$ times a noise standard deviation, so it scales with how noisy
the data are:

```{r rules}
outlier_sd(k = 3.5, sd = "reference")   # trimester reference SD
outlier_sd(k = 3, sd = "iterative")     # SD estimated from the data
outlier_fixed(6)                        # the original fixed cutoff, in nmol/L
```

The default, `outlier_default()`, uses the reference SD for data labelled T1, T2
or T3 and the iterative estimate otherwise. The iterative estimate first sets
aside samples whose absolute residual exceeds 2.75 times the scaled median
absolute deviation of the residuals (`stats::mad()`, which includes the usual
factor 1.4826), refits, and takes the residual SD of that fit. It is meant as a
first pass that removes clearly aberrant samples.

Both multipliers were chosen so that the cutoff for second-trimester data is
close to 6 nmol/L, the cutoff of the original analysis. With the reference SD,
the cutoffs are 4.7, 6.2 and 6.8 nmol/L in the first, second and third
trimesters, matching the noise level of each.

## Why not the residual SD of the initial fit

Two other scales are available, `sd = "model"` (the residual SD of the initial
fit) and `sd = "mad"` (the scaled median absolute deviation of its residuals).
Both are estimated from the fit to the data being cleaned, so they can change
with the amount of contamination. In our development simulation (three cohorts
of 100 per trimester; strong contamination adds 8-12 noise SDs to 10% of
samples), with multipliers calibrated in the same way:

| Scale (k) | Mean cutoff, clean / strong contamination | Spikes missed, strong contamination | Clean samples removed, no contamination |
|---|---|---|---|
| reference (3.5) | 5.9 / 5.9 nmol/L | 24% | 0.11% |
| iterative (3) | 4.5 / 6.0 nmol/L | 25% | 0.35% |
| model (1.75) | 3.2 / 10.2 nmol/L | 43% | 2.6% |
| mad (2.75) | 3.1 / 8.7 nmol/L | 35% | 3.7% (6.1% in the first trimester) |

These figures are specific to that simulation and those multipliers. Neither
`"model"` nor `"mad"` is used by default, but both can be chosen.

## Exploring trade-offs

`tune_threshold()` re-applies different multipliers to the saved initial
residuals of a study. Nothing is refitted, so it is fast, but it reports only
detection errors, not curve recovery.

```{r tune}
runs <- readRDS(system.file("extdata", "vignette-runs.rds", package = "cortisol.nmea"))
tn <- tune_threshold(runs, k = seq(2, 6, by = 0.5), sd = "reference")
d2 <- tn$summary[tn$summary$scenario == "D2", ]
round(d2[, c("k", "cutoff", "FPR", "FNR")], 3)
```

```{r tune-plot}
plot(d2$FPR, d2$FNR, type = "b", pch = 19, xlab = "False positive rate (clean samples removed)",
     ylab = "False negative rate (spikes kept)")
text(d2$FPR, d2$FNR, d2$k, pos = 4, cex = 0.8)
```

The function does not pick a threshold. To compare thresholds by curve recovery
and retention, fit each one:

```{r grid, eval = FALSE}
design <- sim_design(trimesters = c("T1", "T2", "T3"), n = 100, seeds = 1:10,
                     scenarios = c("D0", "D2"),
                     methods = methods_threshold_grid(c(3, 3.5, 4), sd = "reference"))
runs <- sim_run(design, cache_dir = "threshold-cache")
eval_summary(runs)$summary
```

Choose the comparison criteria before looking at the results, and report
retention with recovery.
